column2: Propaedeutics of Internal Diseases: an interactive simulator for cardiac inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, pulse, arterial blood pressure and acquired valvular heart disease

An interactive practice session on the physical examination of the cardiovascular system. Palpate a virtual patient, find the heart borders by percussion, listen to heart sounds and murmurs, measure arterial blood pressure by the Korotkoff method, and learn to tell mitral from aortic valve defects.
Compiled by: Asadbek Axmatkulov · ALVORA · Tashkent State Medical University, Faculty of General Medicine No. 2, 3rd year · 2026
Practical sessions 10–14 of the KTR: cardiac inspection and palpation, percussion and pulse, auscultation, rheumatic fever and mitral defects, infective endocarditis and aortic defects.
Normal phonocardiogram: at the apex S1 is louder than S2, systole is shorter than diastole
Listen with headphones: heart sounds are low-frequency and are poorly heard on a phone speaker. Sounds are synthesized in real time in the browser.
Examine the patient: palpate, percuss, listen

Choose a method and a patient (17 patients). In palpation, click a point: the graph shows how to palpate, what is felt under the palm, and when the impulse and thrill occur relative to the carotid pulse. In percussion, click anywhere on the chest: the percussion note sounds. In auscultation, listen to the 5 standard points and the areas where murmurs radiate. In practice mode the patient's diagnosis is hidden, and you find it yourself.
Projection of the heart and valves
Select a point in the picture.
Graph over time of the carotid pulse and of the impulse and thrill under the palm
Apex beat, cardiac impulse and the “cat's purr”
First palpate approximately with the palm between the 3rd–6th ribs, then precisely with 2–3 fingertips. In women the breast is displaced upward and to the right.
Practice: where is the apex beat?
Choose a patient and click on the chest where the apex beat should be. The program tells you which intercostal space you chose and the distance relative to the midclavicular line.
Click the correct place on the chest.
5th intercostal space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line
Shifted left: left ventricular dilatation. Shifted left and down (6th–7th space): aortic regurgitation
High: thyrotoxicosis, fever, dilatation; low: obesity, pericardial effusion
Resistant, “dome-shaped”: aortic stenosis, arterial hypertension, aortic regurgitation
The 5 features of the apex beat: Location, Area, Height, Force, Resistance.
2nd space, right of the sternum; radiates to the neck
A “cat's purr” is always a sign of an

defect. To determine its phase, the pulse over the carotid artery is palpated at the same time: a thrill coinciding with the pulse is systolic, a thrill coinciding with the pause after the pulse is diastolic.
Taps against the fingertip, increases on inspiration
Taps against the palm surface from above downward, decreases on inspiration
The whole liver expands and contracts: tricuspid regurgitation
Find the heart borders by ear

The pleximeter finger is placed parallel to the border and moved from the clear sound toward the dull sound. Sequence: right, upper, left border. Click each point, choose the first place where the sound changes and press “Border is here”. When all three borders are found, the heart configuration is drawn.
4th space, 1–1.5 cm outside the right sternal border
Left atrial appendage, pulmonary artery conus
5th space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line
Relative dullness “4-3-5”: right border in the 4th space, upper border at the 3rd rib, left border in the 5th space. Transverse diameter 11–13 cm. Vascular bundle in the 2nd space 5–6 cm.
Whichever border is displaced, that chamber is enlarged:
right border — right atrium, upper — left atrium, left — left ventricle.

The heart is auscultated with the patient standing, supine and lying on the left side, in held inspiration and held expiration. The bell of the stethoscope is used for low-frequency sounds (S3, S4, the murmur of mitral stenosis), the diaphragm for high-frequency ones.
Cardiac apex (5th space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line)
Base of the xiphoid process, slightly to the right
Botkin–Erb point: where the 3rd–4th ribs join the sternum, on the left
Order: Mitral — Aortic — Pulmonary — Tricuspid — Botkin.
Library of sounds and triple rhythms
Diagram on the card: phonocardiogram of the sound
Listen to the murmur and describe it
A murmur arises when blood flow is turbulent: when an orifice narrows, when blood flows backward through an incompetent valve, when blood viscosity falls, or when flow accelerates.
systolic or diastolic (compared with the carotid pulse)
does it start after the sound or “swallow” it
the point where it is heard best
along the direction of blood flow
Dependence on position, breathing and exertion
Each murmur sounds at its epicenter

To hear a diastolic murmur well: in mitral stenosis the patient lies on the left side (bell, at the apex); in aortic regurgitation the patient leans forward and holds expiration (diaphragm, at the Botkin–Erb point). Almost any diastolic murmur is organic.
How the pulse wave feels under the finger
Choose the pulse type. The graph shows the pulse wave in the radial artery, and the small lines above it are the heart contractions. The circle shows the beat under the finger.
Pulsus differens: mitral stenosis (Popov–Savelyev sign), aortic aneurysm
Large: aortic regurgitation; small, thready: aortic stenosis, shock
Fast and high: aortic regurgitation; slow and small: aortic stenosis
Measure blood pressure by the Korotkoff method

First, by the palpatory method, inflate until the pulse in the radial artery disappears, then add another 20–30 mm Hg. Deflate at 2–3 mm Hg/s. Press “Systolic” when the first sound appears and “Diastolic” when the sounds disappear completely.
The sounds take on a murmur-like quality
The sounds are clear and loud again
Diastolic pressure in the case of an “endless tone”

“Auscultatory gap”: between phases I and II the sounds temporarily disappear. If the cuff is inflated without the palpatory method, the lower limit of the gap is recorded as systolic pressure and the pressure is underestimated by 20–40 mm Hg.
Four defects, five methods: in one table
Scroll the table horizontally. The buttons in the Auscultation row sound the defect at its epicenter and at its radiation site.
The sound is chosen at random. Listen and mark the correct answer. Listen again if needed.
In each case, open the stages one by one, listen to the points in auscultation and choose the diagnosis.
Axmatkulov A. Propaedeutics of Internal Diseases: a comprehensive manual, topics 10–14. ALVORA, 2026.
Gadayev A.G., Karimov M.Sh., Axmedov X.S. Propaedeutics of Internal Diseases. Tashkent: Muharrir, 2012.
Mancia G., Kreutz R., Brunström M. et al. 2023 ESH Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension. Journal of Hypertension, 2023;41(12):1874–2071.

The sounds are not real recordings: they are synthesized with the Web Audio API from the physical description of heart sounds and murmurs (frequency, duration, shape, phase). For teaching purposes, the features are slightly exaggerated. They do not replace listening to a real patient or a teacher's explanation.

3 · 2nd space, left of the sternum (pulmonary artery)
4 · Base of the xiphoid process (tricuspid valve)
5 · Botkin–Erb point (3rd space, left sternal border)

Place the palm between the 3rd–6th ribs with its base toward the sternum and the fingers toward the axilla (approximate palpation). When the impulse is found, determine its 5 features with the tips of 2–3 flexed fingers. In women the breast is displaced upward and to the right.
Place the palm transversely on the left sternal border, 3rd–4th spaces. In healthy adults no impulse is felt here; a palpable diffuse impulse indicates right ventricular enlargement.

Direct the fingers from beneath the xiphoid process upward toward the heart; ask the patient to take a deep breath. If it taps against the fingertip — right ventricle; against the palm surface — abdominal aorta.
Place the palm on the 2nd space, right of the sternum. With the other hand palpate the pulse in the carotid artery: if the thrill coincides with the pulse, it is systolic.
Place the palm on the 2nd space, left of the sternum. In pulmonary hypertension the tap of S2 can be felt by the hand here.
Palpate the carotid artery at the level of the thyroid cartilage, on the inner edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Never press both at the same time!
No complaints, came for a preventive examination.
The cardiac region is unchanged. No pathological pulsations are visible. Skin color is normal.
72/min, regular, equal in both arms, well filled, moderately tense.
In the 5th space, 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line; area 1–2 cm², moderate height and force, not resistant.
Carotid pulse is normal, simultaneous with the apex beat.

Relative dullness: right border in the 4th space 1–1.5 cm outside the right sternal border, upper border at the 3rd rib, left in the 5th space 1–1.5 cm medial to the midclavicular line. Configuration is normal, vascular bundle 5–6 cm.
S1 is louder than S2 (about 1.5–2 times). No murmur.
S2 is louder than S1; on inspiration S2 splits briefly (physiological splitting).
S1 is loud, S2 is quieter.
Both sounds are of about equal intensity.
All findings are normal: borders “4-3-5”, S1 loud at the apex, S2 loud at the base, no murmur.
Shortness of breath on exertion, nocturnal cough, occasional blood-streaked sputum, palpitations, easy fatigue.
Facies mitralis: bluish-red patches on the cheeks, cyanosis of the lips. Pulsation is visible at the left sternal border and in the epigastric region.
88/min, regular, small; smaller in the left arm (pulsus differens).
Not displaced (5th space), localized, weak: the left ventricle is small. Diastolic (presystolic) “cat's purr” at the apex: the thrill is felt after the carotid pulse, before the next beat.
Cardiac impulse at the left sternal border in the 3rd–4th spaces: right ventricular hypertrophy.
Epigastric pulsation taps against the fingertip and increases on inspiration: right ventricle.
The tap of S2 may be felt by the hand (pulmonary hypertension).

Upper border up to the 2nd rib (left atrium), right border shifted to the right (right atrium and right ventricle). Left border unchanged. The cardiac waist is smoothed out: mitral configuration. Absolute dullness is enlarged.
“Snapping” S1; opening snap of the mitral valve after S2 (“quail rhythm”). Diastolic murmur: low-pitched, rumbling, intensifying in presystole, not radiating; best heard on the left side.
Accentuated and split S2: pulmonary hypertension.
Opening snap and a quiet diastolic murmur.
The murmur does not radiate to the axilla.
Snapping S1 + opening snap (“quail rhythm”) + presystolic crescendo diastolic murmur at the apex + accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery; borders upward and to the right, mitral configuration.
Shortness of breath on exertion, palpitations, weakness.
Shifted left: in the 5th space 1 cm lateral to the midclavicular line; wide, high, increased.
The tap of S2 may be felt.
Left border to the left (left ventricle), upper border upward (left atrium); the right border shifts to the right later. The cardiac waist is smoothed out: mitral configuration.
S1 sharply decreased; a blowing systolic murmur merging with S1 and occupying the whole of systole; S3.
Accentuated S2 (increased pressure in the pulmonary circulation).
The systolic murmur is transmitted quietly.
The systolic murmur radiates to the left axillary region.
Decreased S1 at the apex + a systolic murmur merging with S1 and radiating to the axilla + accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery; borders to the left and upward.
Squeezing retrosternal pain on exertion, dizziness, fainted twice while climbing stairs, shortness of breath.
Skin is pale, the apex beat is barely visible.
64/min, regular, slow and small (pulsus tardus et parvus).
Slightly displaced to the left, strong, resistant (“heaving”): concentric hypertrophy.
Systolic “cat's purr”: the thrill coincides with the carotid pulse and radiates to the neck vessels.
Pulse rises slowly and is small; the thrill is transmitted.
Left border moderately displaced to the left, cardiac waist deepened: aortic configuration. Vascular bundle slightly widened (post-stenotic aortic dilatation).
S1 decreased, S4; the systolic murmur is transmitted quietly.
Harsh, sawing, diamond-shaped (crescendo–decrescendo) systolic murmur; S2 decreased; early systolic ejection click.
The systolic murmur radiates to the carotid artery.

Harsh diamond-shaped systolic murmur in the 2nd space on the right, radiating to the carotid arteries + decreased S2 over the aorta + systolic thrill + pulsus tardus et parvus; angina pectoris, syncope, shortness of breath.
Palpitations, a sensation of pulsation in the neck, dizziness, shortness of breath on exertion.
Skin is pale. “Dance of the carotids”, de Musset's sign (head bobbing), Quincke's capillary pulse. Apex beat is visible.
84/min, rapid, high and large (pulsus celer, altus, magnus): “water-hammer” pulse.
Displaced to the left and down: in the 6th space 2 cm lateral to the midclavicular line; wide, high, strong, resistant (“dome-shaped”).
The carotid artery pulsates sharply and high (“dance of the carotids”).
Left border sharply displaced to the left and down (left ventricular dilatation), cardiac waist deepened: aortic configuration. Vascular bundle widened.
S1 decreased; the diastolic murmur is transmitted to the apex; presystolic Austin Flint murmur.
S2 decreased; protodiastolic murmur; functional systolic murmur of relative stenosis.
A soft, blowing, decrescendo protodiastolic murmur beginning immediately after S2. It is best heard when the patient leans forward and holds expiration.

Protodiastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point + decreased S2 over the aorta + rapid, high pulse + wide pulse pressure (low diastolic pressure) + peripheral vascular signs; left border to the left and down.
Headache in the occipital region, dizziness, ringing in the ears, “flies” before the eyes.
Face is flushed. The apex beat may be visible.
Slightly displaced to the left, increased, resistant.
Left border displaced 1 cm to the left, cardiac waist slightly deepened: tendency toward aortic configuration. Vascular bundle slightly widened.
Presystolic “gallop” (S4): a hypertrophied, poorly compliant ventricle.
Accentuated S2: over the aorta, S2 is louder than over the pulmonary artery, with a metallic quality.
S2 is quieter than over the aorta.
Accentuated S2 over the aorta + resistant apex beat displaced to the left + S4 + high BP and tense pulse.
Acute rheumatic fever, primary rheumatic carditis
Had tonsillitis 2–3 weeks ago. Temperature 38 °C, migrating pain and swelling in the large joints, palpitations, weakness.
Knee and ankle joints are swollen and red. Skin is pale.
112/min, regular, soft; tachycardia is out of proportion to the fever.
Slightly displaced to the left, decreased, diffuse.
Left border shifted 1 cm to the left (left ventricular dilatation). Other borders normal.
Sounds are muffled, S1 decreased; protodiastolic gallop rhythm (S3); soft, blowing systolic murmur at the apex (relative mitral regurgitation).
A quiet systolic murmur is transmitted.
Association with streptococcal tonsillitis + migrating polyarthritis + signs of carditis: tachycardia, muffled sounds, decreased S1, S3, soft systolic murmur at the apex.
Heaviness in the cardiac region, shortness of breath; the patient has to sit leaning forward.
Neck veins are distended, face is puffy. The cardiac region slightly bulges, the apex beat is not visible.
108/min, small; on inspiration the pulse wave decreases sharply (paradoxical pulse).
Apex beat is not palpable (or is felt very weakly well inside the left border of relative dullness).
Pulse is small, decreases further on inspiration.
Borders enlarged in all directions, cardiac waist absent: trapezoid (triangular) configuration. Absolute dullness almost merges with relative dullness. Vascular bundle widened.
Borders enlarged in all directions, trapezoid configuration + apex beat not detectable + sharply muffled sounds + paradoxical pulse, distended neck veins.
Acute, stabbing pain in the cardiac region: worsens with inspiration, cough and lying on the back, decreases on leaning forward. Low-grade fever.
The patient sits leaning forward. Breathing is shallow.
A rough thrill is felt at the left sternal border (pericardial friction).
The friction rub is transmitted quietly.

Pericardial friction rub: scratching, resembling “walking on snow”, in systole and diastole, does not radiate; intensifies with stethoscope pressure and on leaning forward, persists when the breath is held.
At the left sternal border, in the area of absolute dullness, a scratching, non-radiating friction rub that persists when the breath is held + positional acute pain.
5th space, 1 cm outside the midclavicular line
6th space, 2 cm outside the midclavicular line
Combined mitral valve disease, atrial fibrillation
Shortness of breath on exertion, palpitations and “skipped beats”, cough, leg swelling in the evening. Followed for rheumatic valve disease for 20 years.
Facies mitralis, acrocyanosis, swelling of the shins.
Irregular, waves vary, 84/min; heart rate 100/min: pulse deficit 16.
Slightly displaced to the left (regurgitation component), widened. Diastolic thrill at the apex; no presystolic accentuation because of fibrillation.
The tap of S2 is felt.
Borders enlarged upward (left atrium), to the right (right atrium) and to the left (left ventricle); mitral configuration.
Rhythm is irregular, S1 intensity varies; systolic murmur and diastolic rumble (presystolic accentuation disappears in fibrillation).
The systolic murmur radiates to the axilla.
Both systolic and diastolic murmurs at the apex + irregular rhythm and pulse deficit + accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery; borders upward, to the right and to the left.
Stabbing pain in the cardiac region unrelated to exertion, palpitations and a sense of “skipped beats”, easy fatigue, anxiety.
Asthenic build, tall stature, flat chest, hypermobile joints.
In the usual place, features normal.
Mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur that crescendos up to S2. On standing the click moves closer to S1 and the murmur lengthens.
The click and murmur are transmitted quietly.
The late systolic murmur radiates quietly to the axilla.
Mid-systolic click at the apex + late systolic murmur; sounds and borders unchanged; asthenic build. Confirmation: echocardiography.
Leg swelling, heaviness under the right ribs, abdominal enlargement, weakness. Rheumatic mitral valve disease previously diagnosed.
Acrocyanosis, yellowish-bluish skin tint. Neck veins are distended and pulsate in systole (positive venous pulse). Epigastric pulsation, ascites, leg swelling.
Slightly displaced to the left: the enlarged right ventricle pushes the left ventricle aside; diffuse, weak.
Strong diffuse impulse at the left sternal border and its lower part: right ventricular dilatation.
Epigastric pulsation taps against the fingertip and increases on inspiration; the liver expands as a whole in systole (true liver pulsation).
Neck veins fill in systole: positive venous pulse.
Right border sharply shifted to the right (right atrium), left border slightly to the left (the right ventricle pushes the left aside). Absolute dullness enlarged. Liver enlarged.
Rhythm is irregular; murmur is transmitted quietly.
S1 decreased; the systolic murmur intensifies at the height of inspiration (Rivero-Carvallo sign). The respiratory phase is shown in the player.
The systolic murmur is transmitted and intensifies on inspiration.

Systolic murmur at the base of the xiphoid process intensifying on inspiration (Rivero-Carvallo) + positive venous pulse and liver pulsation + marked shift of the right border + systemic venous congestion.
Shortness of breath even at rest, nocturnal attacks of suffocation, dyspnea worse when lying down (orthopnea), weakness, leg swelling.
Semi-sitting position (orthopnea), acrocyanosis, distended neck veins, leg swelling.
104/min, regular, small; large and small waves alternate (pulsus alternans).
6th space, near the anterior axillary line
Sharply displaced to the left and down, wide, diffuse, low and weak: a dilated ventricle with reduced myocardial contractility.
All borders enlarged: left border in the 6th space near the anterior axillary line, right border to the right, upper border up to the 2nd space. “Bovine heart”.
Sounds are muffled, S1 decreased; protodiastolic gallop rhythm (S3); systolic murmur of relative mitral regurgitation.
S3, murmur of relative tricuspid regurgitation.
All borders enlarged + weak diffuse apex beat displaced to the left and down + S3 (gallop rhythm) + muffled sounds + alternating pulse and signs of heart failure.
Weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath and palpitations on exertion, hair loss, craving to eat chalk. Menstrual periods are heavy and prolonged.
Skin and mucous membranes are pale, nails are brittle and spoon-shaped (koilonychia), cracks at the corners of the mouth.
In the usual place; because of tachycardia the impulses are frequent.
No thrill (a functional murmur has no “cat's purr”).
Sounds are loud (tachycardia); a short, soft, blowing systolic murmur, sounds unchanged.
Soft short systolic murmur (best heard here).
A continuous “venous hum” may be heard over the neck veins.
Quiet, short, soft systolic murmur; sounds and borders unchanged, no thrill + pallor, tachycardia: functional (anemic) murmur. Check hemoglobin and ferritin in the blood.
Palpitations, sweating, heat intolerance, hand tremor, weight loss despite a good appetite, nervousness.
Skin is warm and moist, eyes are bright (exophthalmos), finger tremor, thyroid gland enlarged.
118/min, regular, rapid and high (celer et altus).
Slightly displaced to the left, high, increased, diffuse: hyperkinetic circulation.
Left border shifted 1 cm to the left, other borders normal.
Both sounds, especially S1, are accentuated; functional systolic murmur; tachycardia.
Sounds are accentuated, quiet systolic murmur.
A systolic murmur may be heard over the thyroid gland.
Persistent tachycardia (even in sleep), accentuated sounds, functional systolic murmur, wide pulse pressure + signs of thyrotoxicosis (exophthalmos, tremor, weight loss).
Dizziness, darkening before the eyes, two brief episodes of syncope with convulsions (Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attacks), weakness.
Intermittent large “cannon” waves are visible in the neck veins.
Infrequent, strong impulse: the stroke volume is large with every contraction.
Pulse is infrequent, large; intermittent large waves in the neck veins.
Left border slightly displaced to the left.
Bradycardia (38/min); intensity of S1 varies, occasionally a very loud Strazhesko “cannon sound”.
Infrequent regular pulse (30–40), variable intensity of S1 and Strazhesko's “cannon sound”, syncope attacks. Confirmation: ECG.
Smoker for 30 years. Cough, sputum, shortness of breath on exertion, leg swelling in recent months.
Diffuse warm cyanosis, barrel-shaped chest, distended neck veins; pulsation in the epigastric region.
Apex beat is not detected or is very weak: the hyperinflated lung covers the heart.
Epigastric pulsation taps against the fingertip and increases on inspiration: right ventricular hypertrophy.
The tap of S2 is felt (pulmonary hypertension).
Hyperresonant (box-like) note over the lungs. Absolute cardiac dullness is sharply reduced (emphysema). Right border of relative dullness shifted to the right (right chambers).
Quiet systolic murmur, intensifies on inspiration (relative tricuspid regurgitation).
History of lung disease + diffuse cyanosis + epigastric pulsation (right ventricle) + accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery + reduced absolute dullness and muffled sounds.
S1 is longer and lower and follows the long pause; at the apex it is louder than S2.
Normal sounds: base of the heart
At the base of the heart S2 is louder than S1, shorter and higher-pitched.
The ventricle is underfilled; the valve leaflets close quickly and tightly from a wide-open position.
No closed-valve period, or myocardial contractility is reduced: at the apex S1 is quieter than S2.
Pressure in the aorta is raised or the wall is thickened: S2 is strong, sometimes metallic.
Accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery
Pressure in the pulmonary circulation is raised.
Mitral valve disease, chronic cor pulmonale
Only on inspiration: more blood returns to the right ventricle and the pulmonary valve closes later. The respiratory phase is shown in the player.
Does not depend on the respiratory phase, heard in every cycle.
Pulmonary hypertension, atrial septal defect, right bundle branch block
A ventricle with reduced tone vibrates during rapid filling; with tachycardia a “galloping horse” is heard.
A hypertrophied, poorly compliant ventricle is filled by atrial systole; a low-pitched sound before S1.
Snapping S1 + S2 + mitral opening snap (0.07–0.13 s after S2): a three-beat “quail rhythm”.
Sound conduction is reduced or myocardial contractility is weakened.
Bradycardia, intensity of S1 varies; S1 is very loud when atrial and ventricular systole coincide.
Sounds are irregular, intensity of S1 varies; pulse rate is lower than heart rate (pulse deficit).
Mitral stenosis, coronary heart disease, thyrotoxicosis
Apex; radiates to the left axilla
Systolic, merges with S1, blowing, occupies the whole of systole; intensifies in the left lateral position.
Mesodiastolic, low-pitched, rumbling, intensifies in presystole; preceded by an opening snap.
2nd space on the right; to the carotid arteries
Systolic, harsh, saw-like, crescendo–decrescendo; S2 is decreased over the aorta.
Degenerative calcification, bicuspid valve, rheumatic fever
Diastolic, begins immediately after S2, soft, blowing, decrescendo.
Rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis, aortic dilatation
The systolic murmur intensifies on inspiration: more blood enters the right heart. The respiratory phase is shown in the player.
Apex or over the pulmonary artery
Short, soft, quiet (grade 1–2), sounds unchanged; varies with position and load.
Scratching, in systole and diastole, does not radiate; intensifies with pressure, persists when the breath is held.
Regular, 72/min, moderately full and tense. The wave rises quickly, and there is a dicrotic notch after the peak.
Rapid and high pulse (celer et altus)
The wave rises sharply and falls quickly: a “water-hammer” beat under the finger. Typical of aortic regurgitation (Corrigan's pulse).
Slow and small pulse (tardus et parvus)
The wave rises slowly, its peak is late and low. Typical of aortic stenosis.
On inspiration the pulse wave sharply decreases (systolic pressure falls by more than 10 mm Hg). Cardiac tamponade, exudative and constrictive pericarditis, severe asthma attack.
Large and small waves alternate rhythmically. A sign of severe damage to the left ventricular myocardium.
Atrial fibrillation: the waves are irregular and of different sizes. Contractions after a short diastole do not eject enough blood into the artery, so the pulse rate is lower than the heart rate.
Very rapid, small and poorly filled, barely felt. Shock, collapse, massive blood loss.
Left atrial pressure ↑ → pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular hypertrophy
Volume load on the left atrium and left ventricle, dilatation
Pressure load on the left ventricle, concentric hypertrophy
Volume load on the left ventricle, eccentric hypertrophy and marked dilatation
Early shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis, palpitations
Absent for a long time; shortness of breath, palpitations
Palpitations, pulsation in the neck, dizziness
Facies mitralis, cardiac impulse, epigastric pulsation
“Dance of the carotids”, de Musset's and Quincke's signs
Diastolic “cat's purr” at the apex, weak impulse
Apex beat to the left, wide, strong
Systolic thrill in the 2nd space on the right; the impulse is resistant
Impulse to the left and down, “dome-shaped”
Borders upward and to the right; mitral configuration
To the left and upward; mitral configuration
Sharply to the left and down; aortic configuration
Snapping S1, opening snap, diastolic murmur intensifying in presystole; accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery
Decreased S1, systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla; accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery
Harsh diamond-shaped systolic murmur in the 2nd space on the right, to the carotid arteries; S2 decreased over the aorta
Protodiastolic murmur at the Botkin–Erb point; S2 decreased over the aorta
Pulse is small, pulsus differens, often atrial fibrillation
Pulsus tardus et parvus; narrow pulse pressure
Pulsus celer, altus, magnus; systolic ↑, diastolic ↓↓
Shortness of breath on exertion over the past year, nocturnal cough, blood streaks in the sputum twice, palpitations. As a child she often had tonsillitis, and at age 14 her joints ached.
Bluish-red patches on the cheeks, cyanosis of the lips. Pulsation at the left sternal border and in the epigastric region.
Apex beat in the 5th space, localized, weak. Thrill at the apex: felt after the carotid pulse, before the next beat.
Upper border at the 2nd rib, right border 3 cm outside the right sternal border, left border unchanged. The cardiac waist is smoothed out.
88/min, regular, small, smaller in the left arm. BP 110/75 mm Hg.

Facies mitralis, hemoptysis, diastolic thrill at the apex, a shift of the borders upward and to the right, and a diastolic murmur intensifying in presystole with a “quail rhythm”: mitral stenosis. Accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery indicates pulmonary hypertension. Confirmation: echocardiography (orifice area under 1.5 cm²: significant stenosis).
Shortness of breath on exertion, palpitations, weakness. Had rheumatic fever in youth.
Apex beat in the 5th space 1 cm outside the midclavicular line, wide, strong.
Left border shifted to the left, upper border to the 2nd space; the cardiac waist is smoothed out.

Decreased S1 at the apex, a blowing systolic murmur merging with S1 and radiating to the left axillary region, S3, accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery, and a shift of the borders to the left and upward: mitral valve regurgitation. A functional murmur does not change the sounds and the heart borders are not enlarged.
Squeezing retrosternal pain on exertion, fainted twice while climbing stairs, shortness of breath in recent months.
Apex beat slightly displaced to the left, strong, resistant. Thrill in the 2nd space to the right of the sternum, simultaneous with the carotid pulse.
Left border 1 cm to the left, cardiac waist deepened.
64/min, regular, rises slowly and is small. BP 105/85 mm Hg.

The triad of angina, syncope and shortness of breath, a harsh diamond-shaped systolic murmur in the 2nd space on the right radiating to the carotid arteries with a systolic thrill, decreased S2 over the aorta, pulsus tardus et parvus and narrow pulse pressure: aortic stenosis. Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is an indication for valve replacement.
Palpitations, a sensation of pulsation in the neck, dizziness. Treated for infective endocarditis 2 years ago.
Strong pulsation of the carotid arteries, head bobbing in time with the heartbeat, capillary pulsation under the nails.
